text: Once an organization has more than a handful of repositories, the same question comes up every time: does every one of them really need its own hand-written CI/CD pipeline? This lesson is about reusable pipeline templates — the practice of writing the build, test, scan, and deploy logic exactly once, in one place, and having every repo that needs it reference that one copy instead of owning its own.

Here's how the problem actually shows up. Someone writes a solid pipeline early on, and it gets copied into the next repo, and the next, until it's sitting in three hundred separate files. Each copy drifts on its own — one team adds a caching step, another skips the security scan temporarily and never puts it back. Eighteen months later, nobody can say with confidence what pipeline behavior actually runs where, and fixing a bug means editing hundreds of files instead of one.

GitHub Actions solves this with the reusable workflow. It's a normal workflow file, except it starts with on: workflow_call instead of on: push, and it lives in one dedicated template repo. It declares the inputs and secrets it needs — a node version, an NPM token — and inside it, the required security scan step is just part of the template. Every consumer gets that scan by default; it's no longer something a team has to remember to add.

A consuming repo calls that template with a single uses line, pointing at the template repo and, critically, a version tag — at-v1, not at-main. That distinction matters enormously: pinning to a tag means the consumer's build is reproducible and can't be changed out from under it just because someone pushed a new commit to the template's default branch.

Azure DevOps reaches the same outcome with pipeline templates and the extends keyword. A consuming pipeline declares the templates repository as a resource, pinned to a tag, and then extends a template file instead of copying its steps. Extends is the important word here — it means the consuming pipeline can't quietly skip the steps the template defines, which is exactly what you want when a scan step is meant to be non-optional.

Once a template exists, resist the urge to pile conditional branches into it for every team's quirks — a healthy template exposes a small set of explicit inputs and leaves the rest as sane defaults. Next lesson, you'll treat that template repo itself as a real software dependency, with semantic versioning and a changelog, so a breaking change doesn't silently break every repo that calls it.
